name: Zolpidem (Ambien)

lead: Zolpidem, sold as Ambien, is a prescription sleeping pill that helps you fall asleep faster and sleep longer. In sleep and recovery discussions it is one route to consistent sleep, which people connect to better skin and a less tired face.

It enhances GABA-A receptor activity at the benzodiazepine site and has a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours in healthy adults. It is approved for short-term insomnia, typically two to six weeks. A 2005 review described it as improving sleep with favorable tolerability when used as labeled. Published research concerns insomnia, memory and brain activity, not appearance.

paras: It is taken at bedtime on prescription for short-term insomnia, usually with sleep-hygiene measures. Effects on sleep onset come the same night.

Reported effects include next-day impairment, memory problems, hallucinations, falls and impaired driving. The FDA lowered recommended doses in 2013 and added a boxed warning in 2019 about complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-driving. Tolerance and dependence are reported, and it is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.

angle.text: Zolpidem is a prescription sleeping pill people use to fall asleep faster and get more hours, which they link to better skin and a less tired face. It is approved and studied for short-term insomnia.

lead: Zolpidem, best known under the brand name Ambien, is a prescription sleeping pill. In appearance and physique discussion it is raised as one of the ways to fall asleep and stay asleep, on the chain that more complete sleep supports recovery, training and a rested look. It belongs to the nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics known as Z-drugs, and is prescribed for short-term insomnia, usually for about two to six weeks at the lowest effective dose.[1]

It was introduced in Europe in 1988 by Synthelabo, approved in the United States in 1992 as Ambien (developed with Searle), followed by an extended-release version in 2005 and generics from 2007.[1] It is a US Schedule IV controlled substance and in 2023 was the 54th most prescribed drug in the US, with more than 11 million prescriptions.[1] Guidelines from NICE, the European Sleep Research Society and the American College of Physicians place it behind cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia and sleep-hygiene measures.[1]

Published research on zolpidem concerns insomnia, sleep architecture, memory and brain activity rather than appearance, and regulators have added dose reductions (2013) and a boxed warning on complex sleep behaviors (2019).[1][2] Looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums mention it mainly in sleep threads, usually alongside supplements and other sleep aids.[3][4][5]

subs.h: Sleep and recovery in appearance communities
paras: In forums where users track training, skin, hormones and recovery, zolpidem shows up in questions about getting to sleep. A 2001 T Nation post describes trying Ambien after other users suggested over-the-counter antihistamines, and a 2002 reply from another poster calls it excellent among pharmaceutical sleep drugs and says it does not harm sleep quality, expressing personal opinion.[3][4] A 2015 post listing a user's medications mentions having used zolpidem before switching to another sedative for sleep problems.[5] These are individual accounts, and the pill is generally discussed as a prescription option rather than a supplement. This article does not cover sourcing.

Zolpidem is used for short-term insomnia, in immediate-release, extended-release, sublingual and oral-spray forms.[1] It has also been explored off-label for disorders of consciousness and post-stroke aphasia, with unclear benefit; accounts of brain-injured patients temporarily improving after a dose have circulated online and were discussed on Hacker News.[1][6][6] A 2019 trial compared the orexin antagonist lemborexant with placebo and extended-release zolpidem in people aged 55 and older.[7]

According to Wikipedia, zolpidem shortens the time to fall asleep and may increase slow-wave sleep, and a 2012 review concluded that its effect is nearly as much psychological as pharmacological.[1] A 2005 review described it as improving sleep with favourable tolerability when used as labelled.[2] A 2023 Journal of Family Practice update and a 2018 Pharmacological Reviews article on insomnia drugs beyond benzodiazepines place it among the standard options.[8][9] A 2022 Lancet systematic review and network meta-analysis compared drugs for acute and long-term insomnia treatment, and the 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline reviewed individual insomnia drugs, including those used without an FDA indication.[10][11]

Common effects include headache, drowsiness, dizziness and diarrhea. Next-day impairment can affect driving and increases fall and fracture risk.[1] The FDA issued a safety communication in January 2013 on next-morning impairment, reduced recommended doses (including a 50 percent reduction for women) and in May 2013 advised against alertness-demanding activities the day after extended-release use.[1] The 2015 American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria recommend avoiding it in people 65 and older.[1] A case literature has linked hallucinations to combined use with serotonin reuptake inhibitors.[12]

Sleepwalking, sleep-driving, sleep-eating and similar activities followed by amnesia are a central concern and often occur after the first dose or in the first days. Australia's TGA introduced a boxed warning in February 2008, and in April 2019 the FDA added a boxed warning for serious injuries and deaths and a contraindication for people with a prior episode.[1] A 2006 car incident involving a US congressman drew public attention to the problem.[1]

Tolerance can develop within weeks in some people, and dependence and misuse have been reported. Abrupt withdrawal can cause delirium or seizures, so tapers are typical; overdose can cause coma or death.[1] A 2024 randomized trial in JAMA Internal Medicine tested a masked taper with a behavioral intervention for discontinuing benzodiazepine receptor agonists.[13]

Animal studies showed fetal harm only at very high doses, and use in pregnancy is recommended only when benefits outweigh risks; a study examined placental passage and outcomes.[1][14] A 2017 meta-analysis of observational studies reported a tentative association between hypnotic use and cancer risk, and confounding limits those conclusions.[1]

Zolpidem is a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors at the benzodiazepine site. It binds with high affinity to alpha-1-containing receptors, about ten-fold lower affinity to alpha-2 and alpha-3 and little to alpha-5, which is thought to explain strong sedation with weaker anxiolytic, muscle-relaxant and anticonvulsant effects.[1][15] Research has examined its effects on sleep spindles, brain-network synchrony and histamine and cortical neurons.[16][17]

Oral bioavailability is about 70 percent, protein binding about 92 percent and the half-life 2 to 3 hours. Metabolism is mainly via CYP3A4 (about 60 percent), CYP2C9 (about 20 percent) and CYP1A2 (about 14 percent), producing metabolites not believed to be active.[1] An extended-release formulation is reviewed in a 2006 CNS Drugs article.[18]

No studies have examined zolpidem for appearance outcomes. Research concerns insomnia and cognition. A pharmacology study found that zolpidem increased sleep spindles during a nap and was associated with improved memory consolidation, and a related study reported enhanced recognition of negative and high-arousal memories.[16][17] A 2013 study reported that orexin receptor antagonists promoted sleep at doses that did not disrupt cognition in the way standard sleep drugs did.[19] Later orexin antagonist trials, including a phase 3 comparison of lemborexant with placebo and zolpidem extended release for one month, and a phase 2 trial of daridorexant, used zolpidem as a reference or context drug.[7][20]
Registered trials include a 67-person phase 4 comparison of sublingual and oral formulations in primary insomnia and a 132-person phase 4 comparison of modified-release and standard zolpidem.[21][22]

Zolpidem is a US Schedule IV controlled substance, Class C in the UK and controlled in Canada.[1] The US Air Force listed it as a pill with a six-hour restriction before flying as of 2012, and the Australian swimmers' use at the 2012 London Games caused controversy.[1] Recreational misuse, especially among adolescents, has been reported, and in 2018 the comedian Roseanne Barr attributed a social media post to the drug, which its manufacturer disputed.[1] Brand names include Ambien, Ambien CR, Edluar, Intermezzo, ZolpiMist and Stilnox.[1]
